title: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
summary: Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt said populist economics are "not American" and warned against Republicans who want to ban data centers.
content: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.” “A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.” When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums.. “When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said. “When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.” Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy. “To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.” Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

title: Leader of Democratic AG group to step down after Texas triumph
summary: Sean Rankin led DAGA for a decade, helping Democrats flip five GOP-held attorney general offices.
content: CHICAGO — The head of the Democratic Attorneys General Association is stepping down after a successful 2026 cycle in which their party flipped Republican-held attorney general offices in five states, including the conservative legal powerhouse of Texas. Sean Rankin started as executive director at the group — known as DAGA — in 2016, and oversaw its operations as Democratic attorneys general banded together to challenge the first Trump administration over a range of issues. He became president of the group in 2022 and is credited with raising nearly $250 million for DAGA and its affiliated entities over the past decade. “Since Sean joined DAGA in 2016, the committee has won the majority of their competitive races” against Republicans, “reshaping the map for Democrats,” the group said Thursday. Rankin will stay at DAGA as it conducts a search for his successor. Democrats will take control of at least five additional attorney general offices in January, following wins in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa. Alaska, which just elected a Democratic governor, is also expected to have a Democratic attorney general, since the governor appoints the state's top lawyer. “On Texas, we took the head of the snake. So fundamentally, there will be a change in how the Republican attorneys general have to engage nationally if they do not have Texas at the front,” Rankin told POLITICO in a wide-ranging interview after the midterms earlier this month. “Texas has played an outsized role in the actions taken, in my opinion, against many of the issues that I care about, that the AGs fight for, that we believe the American people support — having Texas not on the other side, that’s a game changer.”

title: Beshear defends Texas strategy
summary: The chair of the Democratic Governors Association has taken fire for not spending enough on Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s race in Texas
content: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear defended his decision not to invest more in Gina Hinojosa’s successful race for Texas governor in an interview with POLITICO, amid criticism that could derail his own potential presidential ambitions. Beshear, the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, took heat this month when Latino Democratic operatives and Hinojosa allies publicly maligned him for failing to do enough to help Hinojosa over the finish line. “There might have been frustration by folks who just really wanted to win that race, but they did, and she did, and we're very excited to have her a part of the DGA room,” Beshear said Thursday. “Did we spend a little more money, say, in Kansas, where we were trying to protect the seat? Yes, but we only won that race by 7,000 votes," he said. In a stunning victory, Hinojosa won Texas by 7 percentage points. Hinojosa’s allies’ say that their calls for the DGA to support her campaign went unanswered for months. Ultimately, the DGA contributed $1.4 million — a far cry from the $19 million the organization invested in Keisha Lance Bottoms’ successful bid to win Georgia’s governorship. But Beshear said the context matters. When the budget for this campaign cycle started at the end of 2024, Democrats had suffered brutal losses. “We built out our map protecting our incumbents,” Beshear said. “We were going to be lucky to get [Arizona Gov.] Katie Hobbs and [Oregon Gov.] Tina Kotek reelected, and we were going to have tough elections, even in places potentially like Pennsylvania.” Democrats Abigail Spanberger in Virginia and Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey both won gubernatorial victories in 2025 on affordability platforms, which helped propel them to victory at a time when the economy had become a key pressure point for voters. Heading into 2026, Beshear said, "what came online were the first set of flips, where the earliest polling indicated it was possible, and those were Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. And so at that point, we already had the largest DGA map ever." “We had a size 10 budget with a size 14 map, and then what happened? Alaska, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas and Florida all became or seemed competitive as well, which meant we had a size 10 budget with a size 16 map," Beshear said. The party flipped six governorships in states that President Donald Trump won. In January, Democrats will control 30 governorships and the majority of state legislative chambers. “So at the end of the day, I think we're judged by results,” Beshear said. “And I get that every campaign wants as much funding as they can, but Gina won in Texas, and I'm excited for her.” While Beshear hasn’t publicly announced a run for president in 2028, he’s already crafting his pitch. “If you look at what we've done in Kentucky, the ability to do that all across this country would be special for so many other communities that deserve better jobs, more accessible health care and a better life for our people,” he said. Despite his role as chair of the DGA, Beshear argues that of all the rumored candidates out there, he would be the “ultimate outsider.” He’s not from “inside the Beltway” or either coast. He would be “a candidate from where the South meets the Midwest,” he said — a governor who has helped “improve and revive a place that the country for many years left out.” Beshear says that Bottoms’ victory in Georgia showed Democrats can win in the South. “I am a Southern governor that has won in a red state, and so I knew a great candidate when I saw one,” he said. “And together, our financial support plus her grassroots campaign that turned out voters sent a message that the South is winnable and that the Deep South is winnable.” Next up? Mississippi and Louisiana, Beshear said. “You look at Mississippi, where three years ago the election was close and will be again,” he said. “And then, depending on the candidate we get in Louisiana, the governor there has incredibly low approval ratings, and so even though that's going up against an incumbent, I think the seat is very much in play.” In 2023, Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves defeated his Democratic nominee Brandon Presley by 3.24 percentage points. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry took office in January 2024.

title: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
summary: The independent Team Pete PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Pete Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid.
content: Allies of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are launching an independent, grassroots effort urging him to undertake a second presidential campaign ahead of 2028. Team Pete PAC will be led by Jennifer Holdsworth, the former national campaign manager of Buttigieg’s unsuccessful 2017 bid for DNC chair, and Mohsin Syed, his former chief of staff at the Transportation Department. The PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid. “Mohsin and I have traveled the country this year, and everywhere we go, people ask us the same question: how can I help Pete?” Holdsworth said in a statement. Team Pete PAC is independent and has no ties to Buttigieg’s Win the Era PAC, nor is it a presidential committee. Through Win the Era, Buttigieg campaigned with 102 candidates across the map for the midterms, visiting 38 states (19 of them twice). Asked on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday whether he had a timeline to make a decision, Buttigieg said he would be “surprised” if he was the first potential 2028 presidential candidate “to make news” and said he’s “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.” Even as it forms to press Buttigieg to mount a second presidential campaign, Team Pete PAC is urging potential backers to take part in community service — a nod to Buttigeig’s proposed national service program he proposed as a candidate. “I’ve seen up close what Pete can do,” Syed said. “He has a unique ability to bring people together and inspire action.”

title: JD Vance slams GOP governor’s call for immigration reform as ‘morally and electorally disastrous’
summary: The vice president took aim at Oklahoma Republican Kevin Stitt’s comments at the POLITICO Pub.
content: Vice President JD Vance took aim at Kevin Stitt, calling the Republican governor of Oklahoma’s push for bipartisan immigration reform “morally and electorally disastrous.” “I like Kevin, but what does ‘bipartisan immigration reform’ mean?” Vance wrote on X on Thursday morning. “If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I'm all ears,” Vance wrote. “But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws. It is morally and electorally disastrous.” The vice president was responding to comments the Oklahoma Republican made at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Park City, Utah, on Wednesday. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt said. Stitt described President Donald Trump as a “businessperson” who “understands the need for a workforce.” “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy,” the Oklahoma governor said. But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It’s not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they’re winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That’s why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.” Asked about Vance’s comments on Thursday, Stitt told POLITICO he was “super pumped that the vice president is being engaged in the conversations.” “The governors have been leading on this,” Stitt added. “Republican governors, Democrat governors, have a lot to say on immigration policy, and I am glad the vice president is listening.” Stitt has long called for sweeping changes to immigration policy, including enabling state governors to issue work permits to unauthorized immigrants. Vance – who is weighing a run for the White House in 2028 – has been a staunch defender of the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration. Trump has signaled he is open to cutting a deal on immigration reform in the wake of his party’s midterm defeats. The president told CBS News’s “60 Minutes” earlier this month that his deportation policy was “ too tough ” and had hurt Republicans with some midterm voters. But any agreement still seems unlikely. The same day he spoke to “60 Minutes,” Trump named immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff. Asked about the possibility of a deal earlier this week, Trump told reporters at the White House: “It would be wonderful, but we’ll see.” The president said any agreement would “have to be tough” and offer “no amnesty” for unauthorized immigrants.
authors: By Lauren Fedor and Neha Sati

title: ‘They should be subsidizing the ratepayers’: NC governor says data center subsidies should be rolled back
summary: Democratic Gov. Josh Stein also said the federal government needs to do more to assist with Hurricane Helene recovery.
content: North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein said his state needs to roll back subsidies for data centers, telling POLITICO that Big Tech companies should be “paying their own way.” “I think the idea that this industry needs any public incentive is laughable. These are the wealthiest companies in the history of humanity. They have more resources than many nations. So we, little North Carolina, should not be giving subsidies,” Stein said in an interview Thursday at the POLITICO Pub at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. The Democratic governor pointed to subsidies in North Carolina for electricity for data centers that were rolled back earlier this year , along with ongoing subsidies for the purchase of new equipment, which he said ought to be phased out. “For new data centers, why are we giving them any public dollar when they should be subsidizing the ratepayers?” he said. Stein, elected in 2024, will be governing with a divided Legislature next year after Democrats flipped North Carolina’s House of Representatives this year and broke the Republican supermajority in the state Senate amid a nationwide blue wave . Republicans are likely to maintain narrow control of the upper chamber pending a recount in a pivotal race. The first-term governor, who won by nearly 15 points in 2024 despite President Donald Trump also winning the state that year, didn’t commit to running again in 2028 but said he “cannot think of any” reasons not to. Stein touted bipartisan work in the state to address recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated western North Carolina in 2024. But he faulted “one of the most ineffectual Congresses in history” for failing to deliver for the state. The $60 billion in damages North Carolina suffered, he noted, are nearly as large of a sum as the state’s two-year budget — making it impossible for the state to allocate enough funds for recovery. He said that he spoke to Trump earlier this year and was told that hurricane recovery was a priority for the president, but the necessary federal funds have not come through. “The state stepped up,” Stein said. “The people of Western North Carolina have truly stepped up, and it's time for the federal government to step up.”

title: Keisha Lance Bottoms says Democrats better spend big on the South
summary: Georgia's new governor says Democrats shouldn't have to ‘beg and borrow’ to get resources for campaigns in the South.
content: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said the midterm election results “have spoken for themselves” in showing the need for the Democratic Party to invest more in the South. “I would hope that in two years, we're not having to beg and borrow to be able to run successful campaigns,” Bottoms said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. Democrats had a historically strong cycle in Georgia this year: Bottoms became the first Democrat to win her state’s governorship in more than a quarter-century, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection handily, and the party flipped the state House for the first time in more than two decades. But it wasn’t just Georgia. Democrats also won Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, three states that have long been out of reach for the party, and just missed in Louisiana. “The numbers have been there for Democrats to flip that seat in Mississippi for a while, but the investment has not been there,” Bottoms said. She said that her campaign was a lean operation, particularly in contrast to her GOP opponent’s. Rick Jackson spent nearly $200 million of his own money on his campaign. “During the primary it was the shoestring, dental floss campaign, we were holding it together with every single thing that we had because we weren't getting in the resources and some people have written Georgia off,” she said. “But also even when those resources come from our friends nationally: Trust us. Nobody knows their community, nobody knows their electorate better than the people who are living and breathing it every single day.” Bottoms made history as the first-ever Black woman ever elected governor to in the U.S. earlier this month. But on her campaign trail, she did not focus on the historic nature of her candidacy. “I wake up as a Black woman every day,” she said. “So it was not something that I felt compelled to talk about, it was never top of mind, so it was not even a conscious decision for me not to talk about it. I just didn’t think about it.” She said she instead focused on voters’ cost of living concerns that dominated the cycle. “For me, it was about focusing on the issues. I can't hide, and don't want to hide, that I'm a Black woman,” she said. “To the extent that the conversations were organic with me as a mother or as a woman or whatever the case may have been, then it was a part of the discussion. But I can tell you, as I moved around the state of Georgia, people were focused on, ‘what are you gonna do about this cost of living? How are you going to make my life better?’”

title: Massachusetts gov says Dems want ‘a uniter and a fighter’ for 2028
summary: Democrat Maura Healey just won her second term as governor.
content: Democrats want fighters. Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey believes they want healers, too. Healey, a Democrat who easily won a second term in the deep-blue state earlier this month, told POLITICO on Thursday that she’d like to see her party’s next presidential nominee show “decency” and “humanity.” “It’s really important that we have leaders who genuinely see people, understand their situation. If you don't see people, if you don't understand people, you're never going to be able to deliver for them,” Healey said during an interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “Having leaders who have that, and who have a strong moral compass, I think that's really important,” she told POLITICO’s Adam Wren. Healey suggested the midterms offered a “resetting” as the nation moves toward a post-Donald Trump era. Pressed on whether it’s more important for Democrats to nominate a fighter or a healer, Healey — who burnished her national profile as a hard-charging state attorney general who sued the first Trump administration dozens of times and urged Democrats to more aggressively oppose his second — insisted good leaders can do both. “You can be a uniter and a fighter; you can be a fighter and a healer,” she said. It’s a debate that’s already driving the earliest stages of Democrats’ shadow 2028 primary as the party’s rising stars try to discern whether voters who powered their midterm wave want a brawler or a uniter after candidates of both stripes won difficult races. Healey ruled out a 2028 presidential bid of her own on Thursday. And she deflected when asked whether Democrats should nominate a governor. But the Massachusetts governor, who has close relationships with several likely contenders and routinely hits the campaign trail for Democrats in the early primary state of New Hampshire, could play a role in shaping the primary.

title: Nevada's new governor promises legislative blitz on affordability
summary: Democrat Aaron Ford promised to lower prescription drug prices and rein in corporations’ role in the housing market.
content: Nevada Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford is vowing to immediately pass a trifecta of measures that he says will drive down the cost of living when he enters office in the key swing state. “Those are concrete things that immediately can bring some level of effect to this cost-of-living crisis that we're experiencing right now,” Ford told POLITICO’s Megan Messerly in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. The legislative blitz includes a bill to make school breakfast and lunch free for public school students, legislation that would limit the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicare-negotiated price for everybody and new rules aimed at lowering housing costs that would limit the number of homes corporations can purchase. “I've been working with my colleagues already in the Legislature, and we're going to sign bills beginning on Day 1,” Ford said. “We'll be signing bills within the first 30 days to ensure that we can start effectuating some of the promises that I made on the campaign trail. “You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses — cut regulations and make it easier to do business — I think that’s cool, that’s fine, and that’s dandy. But if you could do it for businesses, you could do it for people too,” he also said. The incoming Nevada governor and former state attorney general also emphasized his willingness to work across the aisle — even though the massive Democratic wins in his state earlier this month make it so “I don't need one Republican vote to get something done in my state right now,” he said. Nevada will be the second state to vote in the Democratic primaries in 2028, and Ford said candidates need to come and travel up and down the state before staking out policy positions. “You need to come to Nevada. Period. Point blank,” Ford said. “We’re one of the most diverse states in the nation. If you can convince a Nevadan that you’re worth your salt, you may very well be able to convince the rest of the nation that you are.” And he cautioned Democrats against making assumptions on what Nevadans want and need. “Don’t presume you know what their issues are,” he said. “Don’t be high and mighty and highfalutin and sitting in some ivory tower putting out ideas when you haven’t heard them say to you what their concerns are.”

title: Rob Sand shuts down any talk of 2028
summary: The incoming Iowa governor said he's unlikely to ever consider running for president.
content: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand isn’t indulging any consideration of him as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. Sand, who cemented himself as a rising star in the party by flipping the governor’s seat in Iowa with a commanding 11-point victory, said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum that he’s unlikely to ever consider running for president. “Are you completely taking 2028 off the table?” POLITICO’s Adam Wren asked Sand. “Yes,” he replied. When asked if he would ever consider running for president, Sand curtly replied, “Doubt it.” Sand offered a tongue-in-cheek rebuttal to the suggestion that he could position himself as an influential voice and a power broker in the national conversation ahead of the next election. “Ooh, that sounds exciting,” Sand quipped sarcastically before adding, “I expect to be a governor in 2027 and in 2028.” Sand also declined to weigh in on his preference for who Democrats should nominate in the presidential primaries. Asked to choose between Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — all of whom campaigned for Democrats in Iowa in the midterms — Sand refused to take the bait. “We have forever to go on all of this,” he said. “The people who want to do that, they're going to get in the race. They're going to do things. They're going to say things. We'll learn a lot more. Then we'll have a clear opinion about who should be doing what.” Sand reiterated that he intends to keep Iowa’s Democratic caucuses as the first nominating contest on the calendar despite the Democratic Party removing Iowa from its early state lineup and encouraged Democratic presidential candidates to continue the tradition of visiting Iowa’s state fair next year. “I'm pretty confident that we'll figure something out that means we're following Iowa law, and they're going to be able to do that,” he said.
